title: Daphnis et Chloé, Suite No. 2
hook: Dawn breaks over a Greek meadow, a flute tells an old love story, and the whole orchestra breaks into a wild dance.

painting.title: Set design for Daphnis et Chloé, Act I
painting.collection: Harvard Theatre Collection, Houghton Library, Cambridge, Massachusetts
painting.pairingNote: Bakst’s design for the first production of the ballet in 1912; the same set, a meadow with the grotto of the Nymphs among the cypresses, returns in the last part, where the dawn of this suite breaks.

facts: *Daphnis et Chloé* is a ballet in three parts, which Ravel finished in 1912 after several years’ work, for Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. It tells a story from an ancient Greek romance by Longus: the young goatherd Daphnis and the shepherdess Chloé, their first love, Chloé’s capture by pirates and her rescue by the god Pan.

The premiere was at the Théâtre du Châtelet in Paris on 8 June 1912, conducted by Pierre Monteux, with Vaslav Nijinsky and Tamara Karsavina as the lovers, choreography by Michel Fokine and sets by Léon Bakst. At almost an hour, it is Ravel’s longest work. He called it a “choreographic symphony”.

Ravel made two concert suites from it. Suite No. 2, published in 1913, is the whole of the last part: daybreak, a pantomime and a final dance. In the ballet a wordless chorus joins the orchestra; the suite can be played with it or without it.
The orchestra is very large, with a big percussion section, two harps and celesta, and Ravel uses it with great precision: the sound of dew, birds, a shepherd’s pipes, the sun.
bigPicture.inOneLine: the sun rises and the lovers meet again (I), they act out the story of Pan and Syrinx (II), and everyone dances (III).

movements.heading: Lever du jour
movements.title: Lever du jour
movements.summary: Daybreak at the grotto of the Nymphs. Daphnis lies asleep at the entrance. The only sound is the trickle of dew from the rocks; birds begin to sing, a shepherd passes playing his pipe, and a great melody rises from the depths of the orchestra as the sun comes up. Daphnis wakes and looks for Chloé; she appears, and they fall into each other’s arms. The old shepherd Lammon explains that Pan saved her, in memory of the nymph Syrinx he once loved.

mainIdeas.name: The murmur of water
mainIdeas.description: rippling flutes, clarinets, harps and muted strings, never still.

mainIdeas.name: The dawn melody
mainIdeas.description: a long, slow, rising tune in the low strings, which grows until the whole orchestra sings it.

notice: Listen to how much is happening under the melody: the rippling never stops. Ravel builds a whole landscape of sound, then lets a tune grow out of it.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Paul Paray, the French conductor who led the Detroit Symphony Orchestra for ten years from 1952, recorded the suite for Mercury’s “Living Presence” series in 1961, in the auditorium of Detroit’s Cass Technical High School. On the Spotify album the suite is tracks 4–6, after Debussy’s *Nocturnes*.

movements.heading: Pantomime
movements.title: Pantomime
movements.summary: To thank the god, Daphnis and Chloé act out the story of Pan and the nymph Syrinx. Chloé plays the nymph, wandering in the meadow; Daphnis plays Pan, who declares his love. She runs away and hides among the reeds. In despair Pan cuts some reeds, makes a pipe and plays a sad melody: here the flute has a long solo, one of the best known in the orchestral repertoire. Chloé dances to it, faster and faster, and falls into Daphnis’s arms. Before the altar of the Nymphs he swears his love.

mainIdeas.name: The nymph’s music
mainIdeas.description: a delicate oboe tune, light and wandering.

mainIdeas.name: Pan’s flute
mainIdeas.description: a long, free solo, sad at first, then more and more agile and whirling.

notice: The flute solo is written very freely, almost like an improvisation. Listen to how the orchestra falls silent around it, then slowly joins the dance.

movements.heading: Danse générale
movements.title: Danse générale
movements.summary: The final dance, a bacchanal for everyone on stage. It is in five beats to the bar, which gives it a limping, breathless energy. Fragments of earlier themes flash past, the music rushes on without a pause, and the work ends with a huge explosion of sound.

mainIdeas.name: The dance rhythm
mainIdeas.description: rapid swirling figures in groups of five beats, hammered out by the whole orchestra.
A flash of the lovers’ music in the middle, swept along by the dance.

stops.hear: Rapid, swirling runs, then a quick, stamping rhythm in five beats
stops.happening: The bacchanal begins

stops.hear: The brass take up the dance; the percussion grows louder
stops.happening: The dance gathers everyone in

stops.hear: A brief, lighter moment, then the swirling starts again
stops.happening: A breath before the last rush

stops.hear: The whole orchestra, louder and faster, wave after wave
stops.happening: The final build

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A last huge chord with crashing percussion
stops.happening: The end of the ballet

notice: Try to count the five beats in each bar. The extra beat makes the dance feel always slightly off balance, like dancers who cannot stop.

threads.title: A day in one suite
threads.body: The suite runs without a break from first light to the height of the celebration, from the softest sound in the orchestra to the loudest.

threads.title: Nature in sound
threads.body: Water, birdsong, a shepherd’s pipe, the sun: Ravel paints each one with exact instrumental colours, never with vague washes.

threads.title: One love story inside another
threads.body: The young lovers act out an older love story, Pan and Syrinx, and the flute is both Pan’s reed pipe and the voice of their own feelings.
